SEC-HD-V8-01.note: 2x2 number x tense. Head is 'shipment' (singular); 'since the war' licenses present perfect. Only item in the batch where present perfect is right.

SEC-HD-V8-02.note: Supplement opened with a comma must close with a comma, so dash options die on shape; 'east range' singular. The singular predicate nominative 'the only stretch' sits immediately after the blank and hints the number on its own.

SEC-HD-V8-03.note: 'who' is subject of 'had falsified' (A and C use whom). But B and D are BOTH internally consistent punctuation; only the restrictive/nonrestrictive reading separates them, and D is defensible if the reader takes 'the partner' as already identified. Genuine second answer under the supplement convention - this is the item I would pull.

SEC-HD-V8-04.note: Dangling participle: only 'the observer' can have lost the count. Tense then kills D (1898 narrative, 'came home').

SEC-HD-V8-05.note: 'not only X but also Y' correlative plus noun-phrase parallelism after 'cut'. B is eliminable on the correlative alone without reading the passage; D's 'but it also' is eliminable on shape.

SEC-HD-V8-06.note: 'more than one of the twelve tenants' takes a singular verb in edited usage (Garner), and the frame is past. But 'more than one of' + plural noun with notional plural agreement ('were turned away', C) is accepted by several usage authorities; not merely a folk usage. Flagging honestly.

SEC-HD-V8-07.note: DEFECT: with 'that still' inside every option, 'survive' is consumed by the relative clause and the resulting sentence has no main verb - all four options yield a fragment. Separately, C and D are eliminable without the passage (no comma before restrictive 'that'), leaving a bare apostrophe coin-flip; two surveyors -> plural possessive.

SEC-HD-V8-08.note: Head 'cellar' singular; 'smell' is a linking verb taking the predicate adjective 'sweet'. Clean 2x2. The later 'smells of nothing' confirms but is far past the blank.

SEC-HD-V8-09.note: 'each of the four pits' singular; 'already' before a 1861 reference point wants past perfect passive. D is number-correct and voice-correct, only tense-wrong, so it is the live distractor - close but not defensible.

SEC-HD-V8-10.note: Gerund-phrase subject is singular; 'In the years the wharf was in use' is a closed past frame, so present perfect is out.

SEC-HD-V8-11.note: 'as well as' phrase does not change number of 'The march'; 'when the bandmaster retired' fixes simple past.

SEC-HD-V8-12.note: 'along with' intervener; head 'tracings' plural, and the active progressive 'were/was losing' is near-eliminable without the passage since tracings do not lose. Easiest item in the set.

SEC-HD-V8-13.note: Three-item infinitive series 'to sample, to weight, and to record'.

SEC-HD-V8-14.note: Verb is settled ('type' singular, past frame), so it comes down to its/their. I read the possessor as 'a mission' (singular). But 'their remaining type' referring to the two presses (A) is a legitimate reading - the presses are the grammatical subject of the preceding clause and are the things type belongs to. Second answer defensible under ordinary antecedent choice.

SEC-HD-V8-15.note: 'contains,' opens an interrupter that must close after 'themselves'; C's extra comma after 'list' severs the object from its 'of' phrase.

SEC-HD-V8-16.note: Appositive 'a volume rebound so often that its earliest leaves are out of order' must close with a comma before the main verb 'records'; a colon cannot stand between subject and verb.

SEC-HD-V8-17.note: DEFECT: three of the four options legally punctuate the clause boundary. B (period + 'Consequently' with no following comma) and C (semicolon + 'consequently' with no comma) are both accepted edited English - the comma after a conjunctive adverb is conventional, not obligatory. Nothing in the passage selects D over B or C. Second answers: B and C.

SEC-HD-V8-18.note: 'not only A but also B' agrees with the nearer subject 'the village schoolmaster'; past frame. Same special-subject family as item 06.

SEC-HD-V8-19.note: 'The remains' plural; the present-tense 'what is left' at the end of the sentence fixes present tense, but that is far after the blank.

SEC-HD-V8-20.note: Head 'clauses' plural across a long relative-clause intervener ('act ... a wagon ... width'); closed past frame kills the perfect options. Structurally near-identical to item 01 with the number reversed.

SEC-HD-V8-21.note: Third conditional: 'would have collapsed' in the main clause forces past perfect in the if-clause. A is eliminable on shape (would-have in both halves).

SEC-HD-V8-22.note: Comma after the fronted 'Because' clause; 'the yard had fitted' is a restrictive relative and must not be bracketed.

SEC-HD-V8-23.note: Backshift after 'reported in 1889' rules out 'will'; 'exhaust' is not used intransitively of a seam, so the voice test does half the work and B/D are close to shape-eliminable.

SEC-HD-V8-24.note: 'one of the very few works ... that credit' - the relative modifies plural 'works'. C and D die without the passage on the comma-before-'that' rule, so the item is effectively a two-way choice. Same template as item 07.

heuristics_found.rule: In the 2x2 number-x-tense quartets, eliminate the present-perfect pair ('has been X' / 'have been X') unless the passage carries 'since'. The passages are all dated historical narrative with closed past frames.
heuristics_found.fired: 6 of the 7 quartet items (06, 09, 10, 11, 18, 20); it FAILS on 01, which is the one passage containing 'since the war' and is keyed to the perfect. Halves the option set on those items without engaging the actual agreement test.

heuristics_found.rule: In punctuation items, prefer the option with the FEWEST commas that still closes an opened supplement.
heuristics_found.fired: held on 07, 15, 16, 22, 24 - 5 of the 7 punctuation items. The extra-comma option (15C, 22D, 16D) is a recurring shape.
eliminates two of four options in 07 and 24 with the passage covered. Not a key-picking tell, but it makes both items two-way guesses at 50 percent blind.

heuristics_found.rule: Longest option / hedged option / comma-bearing option.
heuristics_found.fired: tested and did NOT hold; key lengths and comma-presence look unpatterned to me.

cross_item_heuristic.answer_sequence_impression: Letter distribution across my 24 picks is A5 B6 C7 D6, and I saw no run or slot bias while working. I did NOT develop a letter-level tell. The real exposure here is structural, not positional: 9 of 24 items are the same subject-verb-agreement-across-an-intervener template, so a solver who learns 'find the head noun, ignore the of/along with/as well as phrase' clears more than a third of the batch with one idea. Blind (source covered) I would expect roughly 25-35 percent on the quartets - the option sets alone do not name the subject - but 50 percent on 07 and 24 from the comma-before-'that' shape alone.

template_groups.shared: plural/singular head separated from the verb by a long modifier; identical 4-option shape was/were/has been/have been + past participle. Near-duplicates with the number flipped.
'as well as' / 'along with' intervening phrase that does not change the subject's number. Solving one gives the other.
special-subject agreement ('more than one of' / 'not only ... but also'), same 4-option tense-x-number shape.
singular subject that looks plural ('each of the four pits' / gerund phrase over a plural object) plus a tense-depth choice.
agreement quartet where the second axis is not tense (adjective/adverb; present/past) - the mildest pair.
comma-before-restrictive-'that' as the throwaway axis, with the real axis (apostrophe placement / relative-clause agreement) on the remaining two options. Same construction twice.
matched-punctuation supplement: an opened comma or dash must be closed in kind, with an extra-comma decoy.
series/correlative parallelism with one option breaking into a finite clause.
backshift/conditional tense sequencing after a reporting or counterfactual frame.
